meta.description: Nearly C.S. Lewis: The Four Loves (1960), ch. IV. He wrote "one man", and the familiar ending is spliced in from his own earlier sentence.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Friendship is born at that moment when one person says to another, "What! You too? I thought I was the only one."'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely C.S. Lewis, from The Four Loves (1960). The popular version splices two of his sentences and quietly changes "one man" to "one person".

answer.label: Not quite — Lewis wrote “one man”, and the ending is from another sentence
answer.authorDates: 1898–1963 · Oxford and Cambridge literary scholar, novelist and Christian apologist
answer.sourceLine: The thought and the words are Lewis’s, from chapter IV of The Four Loves (1960), the chapter on Friendship. Wikiquote’s sourced section carries two sentences from that chapter. The first: “Friendship arises out of mere companionship when two or more of the companions discover that they have in common some insight or interest or even taste which the others do not share… The typical expression of opening Friendship would be something like, ‘What? You too? I thought I was the only one.’” The second, later in the same chapter, is Lewis recapping himself: “Friendship, I have said, is born at the moment when one man says to another ‘What! You too? I thought that no one but myself…’” The version people quote is the recap’s opening welded to the first sentence’s punchline — which is to say it finishes Lewis’s own trailing ellipsis with Lewis’s own words, and changes “one man” to “one person”. We keep a separate page for the sentence as Lewis wrote it, which is verified.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed as worded — the book and chapter are certain, the sentence is spliced from two of his

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 1960, by Geoffrey Bles in London; developed from a set of radio talks Lewis recorded in 1958
Ch. IV, “Friendship” — the third of the four loves, philia

source.excerpt: Friendship arises out of mere companionship when two or more of the companions discover that they have in common some insight or interest or even taste which the others do not share and which, till that moment, each believed to be his own unique treasure (or burden). The typical expression of opening Friendship would be something like, “What? You too? I thought I was the only one.”
trail: The sentence people quote is Lewis’s own recap, which appears later in the same chapter: “Friendship, I have said, is born at the moment when one man says to another ‘What! You too? I thought that no one but myself…’” The trailing ellipsis is Lewis’s, not an editor’s — both sentences are transcribed on Wikiquote ↗.

The two changes. “One man” became “one person” somewhere in the retelling, and the open ellipsis was closed with the phrasing from Lewis’s earlier sentence, “I thought I was the only one.” Both halves are his, from the same chapter; the join is not.

The book. The Four Loves was published in 1960 and grew out of radio talks Lewis recorded in 1958, working through the Greek terms storge, philia, eros and agape in that order — Wikipedia’s article on the book ↗.

What could not be checked. The book is in copyright: the 1960 Harcourt, Brace American edition is on the Internet Archive as a borrow-only scan, and its text is not downloadable, so this page rests on Wikiquote’s sourced transcription rather than on a page image read here — the catalogue record ↗.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed in Wikiquote’s sourced section for The Four Loves ↗, attributed there to chapter IV. Note the two things the popular version loses: Lewis does not say friendship is this moment, he says the moment is its “typical expression” — and his subject is a shared “treasure (or burden)”, which makes the recognition a relief rather than a coincidence.

author.name: C.S. Lewis
author.heading: About C.S. Lewis
author.metaLine: 1898–1963 · Irish-born British literary scholar, novelist and Christian apologist
author.bio: Clive Staples Lewis was born in Belfast in 1898 and spent his working life teaching English literature: nearly thirty years as a fellow and tutor at Magdalen College, Oxford, then the new chair in Medieval and Renaissance Literature at Cambridge from 1954 until his death in 1963. He wrote in three registers at once — scholarship (The Allegory of Love), children’s fiction (The Chronicles of Narnia) and popular theology (Mere Christianity, The Screwtape Letters) — and was a central member of the Inklings, the Oxford writing circle that also gave Tolkien his first readers. The Four Loves, from 1960, is his late attempt to say precisely what people mean by the word love.

misattribution.heading: Right author, adjusted words
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here — the sentence really is Lewis’s, from a book he wrote. What has drifted is the wording, and two of the changes are worth knowing about.

items.why: Lewis wrote “when one man says to another”. The modernised “one person” is an improvement on his 1960 idiom and changes nothing he meant, but it is not what is on the page — compare Wikiquote’s transcription ↗.

items.who: “I thought I was the only one”
items.why: In the sentence that begins “Friendship… is born at the moment”, Lewis trails off: “I thought that no one but myself…” The familiar ending comes from his earlier sentence in the same chapter. Using it to close the ellipsis is faithful to his sense — but it is a join made by quoters, not by Lewis.

Lewis’s more careful formulation is that the moment is Friendship’s “typical expression”, and that friendship “arises out of mere companionship” when companions find a shared treasure or burden. The popular version turns a description of how friendship begins into a definition of what it is.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest summary: this is C.S. Lewis, from chapter IV of The Four Loves (1960), in a tidied and spliced form built entirely out of his own words. Both source sentences are on Wikiquote ↗, and quotle.info has a separate page for the wording Lewis actually wrote.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Lewis was writing against a culture that had quietly demoted friendship. Wikipedia’s account of the book has him observing that to the ancients friendship “seemed the happiest and most fully human of all loves; the crown of life and the school of virtue”, and lamenting that modern society has largely neglected it — see the article ↗. The “What! You too?” moment is his evidence: friendship starts not with attraction or duty but with the discovery that something you assumed was yours alone is shared.

The detail the popular version drops is the most Lewis-like part of it. He does not say the companions discover a shared interest; he says a shared “treasure (or burden)”. Friendship, on his account, can just as easily begin with a confession as with an enthusiasm — and that is why the line lands on anyone who has ever felt like the only one.
detailsBody: The Four Loves began as radio talks recorded in 1958 and was published as a book in 1960. It works through four Greek words in order: storge, the affection of family; philia, friendship; eros, romantic love; and agape, the love Lewis calls charity. Friendship gets the third chapter and, notably, the longest defence, because it is the one Lewis thought needed defending.

Lewis knew the subject from the inside. He was a central member of the Inklings, the Oxford circle in which he, J.R.R. Tolkien and others read each other work in progress — the practical demonstration of the argument the chapter makes.
context.pull: What Lewis wrote was "one man". What he meant was anyone who had been carrying something alone.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote’s sourced section for The Four Loves (1960) transcribes both "The typical expression of opening Friendship would be something like, ‘What? You too? I thought I was the only one.’" and "Friendship, I have said, is born at the moment when one man says to another ‘What! You too? I thought that no one but myself…’", both attributed to Ch. IV.
The Four Loves was first published in 1960 by Geoffrey Bles, developed from radio talks recorded in 1958, and treats storge, philia, eros and agape in that order.
The Internet Archive holds the 1960 New York: Harcourt, Brace edition of The Four Loves, and its full text is restricted rather than downloadable.

C. S. Lewis was born 29 November 1898 in Belfast and died 22 November 1963 in Oxford; he taught at Magdalen College, Oxford (1925–1954) and held the Cambridge chair of Medieval and Renaissance Literature (1954–1963).
